Field-Level EDA Across Three Growers

Boundaries, cropland and weather in Illinois, Iowa and Nebraska

Report date

Period
2021–2025

At a glance

3
growers, one farm each
30
fields, 10 per grower
9,775
acres in scope
5
CDL years, 2021–2025
  • Nebraska is structurally different. Its ten fields are near-equal in size (Gini 0.06), all corn-dominant in 2025, and average 55% continuous corn.
  • Illinois and Iowa are bimodal. Each holds about half its acres in three fields, alternates corn and soybean, and carries three small legacy OpenStreetMap fields alongside large USDA CSB blocks.
  • Weather separates growers, not fields. Seasonal GDD differs across growers (p < 0.001); precipitation does not (p = 0.234). Fields within a grower share NASA POWER grid cells, so field-level weather differences are mostly cell artifacts.

USDA CSB = Crop Sequence Boundaries (FIBOA) parcel polygons. OSM = legacy OpenStreetMap/Overpass farmland polygons retained from Assignment 1. One farm per grower, so grower and farm are the same unit in this analysis.

Comparison levels

LevelUnitWhere it is used
Field30 polygonsSize ranking, acreage concentration, map, per-field summaries.
Field-year150 observationsCrop rotation (5 years), seasonal GDD, seasonal precipitation.
Grower3 groups of 10 fieldsDistributions, Kruskal–Wallis, Mann–Whitney, variance decomposition.
Across-grower3 groupsPairwise tests, Gini permutation tests, three-panel map.

Within-field change over time is read from the two heatmaps (one row per field, one column per year). Across-field comparisons keep the field as the unit and group only by grower.

Analysis choices

  • Growing season: April 1 – September 30. GDD uses a 10 °C base from (T2M_MAX + T2M_MIN) / 2, clipped at zero; precipitation is the season total. This is an agronomic season, not a frost-free definition.
  • Tests: Kruskal–Wallis for a three-group difference, two-sided Mann–Whitney for pairs, Holm step-down adjustment for multiple comparisons, epsilon-squared and rank-biserial effect sizes.
  • Weather unit: grid-cell-year, not field-year. Illinois and Iowa each collapse to two temperature series and Nebraska to one, so field-year rows are pseudo-replicates.
  • Concentration: Gini with 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals and 10,000-permutation tests on Gini differences.

1. Field boundaries

What the comparison shows

TestResultReading
Kruskal–Wallis, all 30 fieldsH = 4.46, p = 0.107, ε² = 0.09Not significant: the six legacy OSM fields mask the cross-grower gap.
Kruskal–Wallis, CSB only (24 fields)H = 17.04, p < 0.001, ε² = 0.72Strong: Illinois and Iowa CSB blocks are larger than Nebraska parcels.
GiniIL 0.32, IA 0.33, NE 0.06IL and IA are concentrated; NE is nearly equal.
Gini permutation, NE vs ILΔ = 0.262, p = 0.010 (Holm 0.021)NE is more even than IL.
Gini permutation, NE vs IAΔ = 0.263, p = 0.003 (Holm 0.008)NE is more even than IA.
Gini permutation, IL vs IAp = 0.993Indistinguishable; the bootstrap intervals overlap.

The pooled test is a good example of why source matters. Across all 30 fields, area does not differ significantly across growers. Remove the legacy OSM fields and the CSB-only test becomes decisive. In other words, part of the apparent cross-grower difference is a data-lineage difference, not a farming difference. The report keeps both results and shows source on every boundary figure.

2. CDL / cropland

What the comparison shows

MeasureResultReading
2025 corn-dominant fieldsIL 5/10, IA 2/10, NE 10/10Composition differs sharply by grower.
Kruskal–Wallis, 2025 corn shareH = 6.74, p = 0.034, ε² = 0.18Overall difference exists, but no pair survives Holm correction because Illinois is bimodal (5 corn, 4 soybean, 1 pasture).
Kruskal–Wallis, continuous cornH = 21.89, p < 0.001, ε² = 0.74The sharpest separation in the dataset.
Continuous-corn frequencyIL 0%, IA 10%, NE 55% meanNE vs IL Holm p < 0.001; Iowa's mean is driven by one field at 100%.
Kruskal–Wallis, 5-year diversityH = 0.56, p = 0.757No difference: nearly every field carries two crops.

Corn share and continuous corn are related measures of corn intensity, so they are treated as one family and corrected together. The diversity null result is informative: all three growers rotate at least occasionally, but Nebraska returns to corn far more often. CDL is a 30 m modeled label, not ground truth, so this is descriptive rotation intensity rather than a management verdict.

3. Weather

What the comparison shows

MeasureRange / testReading
Apr–Sep GDDIL 1,782–1,916; IA 1,557–1,886; NE 1,974–2,196Nebraska is the hottest; northern Iowa is the coolest.
Kruskal–Wallis, GDDH = 14.43, p < 0.001, ε² = 0.57Growers differ; NE vs IL and NE vs IA both Holm p = 0.008.
Apr–Sep precipitationIL 417–632 mm; IA 405–801 mm; NE 340–585 mmIowa has the widest spread; Nebraska is lowest.
Kruskal–Wallis, precipitationH = 2.91, p = 0.234No significant cross-grower difference.
Variance decomposition (ICC)GDD 0.82; precipitation 0.2382% of GDD variance is between growers, but only 23% of precipitation variance.

NASA POWER grid cells in this dataset: Illinois 2, Iowa 2, Nebraska 1, for 25 cell-years. That is why the weather tests use cell-year observations. The honest conclusion is that climate differs by grower location, while field-to-field weather differences inside a grower are not microclimate.

4. Geospatial map

The map puts the crop pattern on the ground and shows where each polygon came from at the same time. Illinois and Iowa mix large CSB blocks with small, irregular OSM fields; Nebraska is a uniform set of CSB parcels. The provenance layer matters because boundary source is confounded with field size: the largest blocks are CSB, and the smallest, most irregular polygons are legacy OSM. Reading the map without that distinction would over-attribute a data-lineage difference to farming.

Headline results

QuestionAnswer
Are field sizes comparable across growers?No. Illinois and Iowa are bimodal with large CSB blocks; Nebraska is ten near-equal parcels. The gap is significant only after removing legacy OSM fields.
Is acreage concentrated?Yes in Illinois and Iowa (Gini 0.32–0.33; top three fields hold 51%). No in Nebraska (Gini 0.06; top three hold 34%).
Does cropping differ?Yes. Nebraska is 10/10 corn-dominant and 55% continuous corn; Illinois is 0% continuous corn; Iowa is 10% with one field.
Does weather differ?GDD yes; precipitation no. Nebraska is hotter, northern Iowa cooler, and precipitation spread is wide everywhere.
What drives the weather signal?Grower location, not field position. Fields within a grower share one or two NASA POWER cells.
What does the map add?Crop geography plus boundary provenance, including the Nebraska all-CSB asymmetry.

Limitations, missing data and assumptions

  • Small sample. Ten fields per grower. Every test is exploratory; read effect sizes and Holm-adjusted p-values, not significance alone. Gini bootstrap intervals are wide (Illinois 0.14–0.50).
  • One farm per grower. Grower and farm are the same unit, so there is no replication at the farm level and no separation of grower effects from local site effects.
  • Weather is grid-cell weather. Illinois and Iowa each have two NASA POWER temperature series and Nebraska one. Field-level weather differences within a grower are largely artifacts, not microclimate. Tests use cell-year observations to avoid pseudo-replication.
  • CDL is modeled. 30 m labels, not ground truth. Five years supports descriptive rotation intensity, not a long-term rotation or yield claim.
  • Boundary sources differ. Illinois and Iowa mix USDA CSB parcels with legacy OSM polygons; Nebraska is all CSB. The analysis reports source and includes a CSB-only sensitivity run. Shape and size comparisons are partly source comparisons.
  • No yield, soil, DEM or satellite data. The report makes no yield, soil, terrain or vegetation claim, and no causal claim about management.
  • Season choice. April 1 – September 30 with a 10 °C GDD base is an agronomic window for corn and soybean; it is not a frost-free definition and excludes post-maturity October.
  • Weather source. NASA POWER is a modeled/reanalysis product, not on-farm sensor data.
  • Missing data. Weather tables have no nulls or duplicate field-date rows. Legacy OSM fields have no crop attribute; CDL supplies the crop label for every field.
Soil analysis was not required. No SSURGO, gNATSGO or SoilGrids input was read, and soil properties are not part of any comparison, test, figure or map in this report. Soil is outside the scope of this assignment.

Reproduction

The reusable workflow lives at my-farm-advisor/eda/eda-field-level; this report is a one-time artifact and is not generated by the subskill. Analysis outputs stay in the runtime; only the curated figures and tables are committed under examples/assignment-2.

export DATA_PIPELINE_DATA_ROOT=~/my-farm-advisor-runtime
cd my-farm-advisor/eda/eda-field-level/scripts
"$DATA_PIPELINE_DATA_ROOT/data-pipeline/.venv/bin/python" run_all.py
"$DATA_PIPELINE_DATA_ROOT/data-pipeline/.venv/bin/python" publish_examples.py
